PROJECT LANTERN 1 — COMMUNITY LIBRARY APPOINTMENT PILOT
Status Report: October 2026 — November 2026

---

ENTRY 1 | 2026-10-03
Project Lantern 1 kicked off on schedule. Scope: a twelve-week appointment-booking pilot for Riverside Branch Library (urban, 240 registered patrons), focused on tech help desk sessions. System integrates with the library's existing patron database and sends SMS/email reminders. Pilot covers three use cases: computer basics, printing assistance, and one-on-one account help. Target: reduce no-shows from current 22% to 15% through reminder automation and confirmation workflows. Technical stack: Python backend, PostgreSQL, Twilio for SMS, SendGrid for email. Team assigned: Dmitri (backend), Sara (frontend), and Marcus (QA). First sprint deliverables: core appointment schema, database migrations, and booking form UI. Kick-off meeting confirmed all three use cases and established working sessions every Monday and Thursday.

---

ENTRY 2 | 2026-10-10
Week 1 build phase complete. Database schema finalized: appointments table holds patron_id, session_type, scheduled_time, status, and created_at. Booking form deployed to staging environment. Initial unit tests passed: patron lookup (8 tests), time-slot availability check (12 tests), and basic form validation (14 tests). No blockers. Sara reported frontend styling issue with mobile date picker—resolved same day. Dmitri integrated Twilio credentials and ran send-test on three library staff email addresses; messages arrived within 4 seconds. Marcus scheduled exploratory manual testing for week 2. Remainder of week focused on error-handling paths and edge cases around patron re-booking within 24 hours (currently returns HTTP 409, intentional to prevent double-booking).

---

ENTRY 3 | 2026-10-17
Week 2 manual testing began on staging. Marcus ran 47 booking attempts across the three use cases: 31 succeeded, 16 hit intentional validation rules (duplicate bookings, out-of-hours slots, invalid patron IDs). No system crashes. SMS reminders queued and delivered for 22 confirmed appointments. One issue found: confirmation email template rendered library address as null in four cases—root cause was missing address field in patron records for recently registered users. Corrected in data fix. Load test on booking endpoint: held 120 concurrent requests without degradation. Dmitri noted database query time at p95 was 187ms under load. Sara added client-side loading spinner to improve perceived responsiveness. Both changes merged to staging. Pilot readiness assessment: 85%.

---

ENTRY 4 | 2026-10-24
Gap discovered during workflow walkthrough. QA scenario: patron books appointment, receives confirmation, then initiates cancellation through the mobile UI. Expected behavior: cancellation request succeeds, patron sees confirmation message, appointment status changes to "cancelled," reminder SMS is suppressed. Actual behavior observed: system accepted cancellation request and updated status to "cancelled," but the reminder was already enqueued in Twilio queue for delivery at scheduled time, and no mechanism existed to dereference or cancel the queued message. In test case, patron received SMS reminder for an appointment they had cancelled 36 hours prior. Critical issue. Cancellation-flow implementation was incomplete—only the database update was implemented; message-queue integration was deferred. This gap affects all three use cases. Impacts: user experience broken, patron trust compromised, SMS costs incurred for unused messages. Estimated scope: medium complexity, low risk.

---

ENTRY 5 | 2026-10-26
Root-cause analysis completed. Issue stemmed from sprint planning ambiguity: cancellation was assigned as "UI + Database," and message-queue reversal was treated as separate, unassigned work. No code review caught the incomplete flow because reviewers checked status-field logic in isolation. Twilio API supports message dereference (cancel outbound message by ID before delivery), but our system never stored the Twilio message ID. Repair approach: (1) store Twilio message_id when reminder is first enqueued, (2) add cancellation handler that looks up message_id and calls Twilio cancel endpoint, (3) add integration tests for the full cancellation flow, (4) add client-side confirmation dialog so patron cannot accidentally cancel. Estimated effort: 18 hours backend, 6 hours frontend, 8 hours testing. Repair begins week of 2026-10-28. No timeline impact if completed by 2026-11-02.

---

ENTRY 6 | 2026-10-28
Repair work started. Dmitri added message_id field to appointments table, ran migration on staging, and wrote storage logic to capture Twilio response on reminder enqueue. Query tested manually: SELECT message_id FROM appointments WHERE id = 1 returned correct 32-character hex ID. Schema change merged. Sara implemented cancellation confirmation modal on frontend with two-button layout (Confirm Cancellation / Keep Appointment). Styling matches existing UI. Marcus prepared integration test cases. Blocker encountered: Twilio API credentials expired in staging environment; re-issued same day. No delay to schedule.

---

ENTRY 7 | 2026-10-31
Cancellation handler implemented and deployed to staging. Dmitri added endpoint POST /appointments/{id}/cancel that retrieves message_id, calls Twilio cancel API, checks HTTP 204 response (success), updates appointment status to "cancelled" and sets reminder_sent to false. If Twilio call fails, logs error but completes database transaction to ensure appointment is marked cancelled (eventual consistency; async cleanup task retries Twilio cancel every 5 minutes for 1 hour). Test of happy path: booked appointment, triggered cancel within 20 minutes of scheduled time, received 204 from Twilio, appointment status confirmed as "cancelled." Reminder delivery simulated—no SMS sent. Tested also: cancellation attempt on appointment already past (HTTP 400, proper error message). Tested: cancellation when message already delivered (Twilio returns 404, handled gracefully). All three pathways working. Code merged to staging.

---

ENTRY 8 | 2026-11-02
Full integration testing of cancellation flow completed. Marcus executed 34 test cases covering: (1) cancel within 1 hour of appointment (11 cases)—all cancelled, no reminder sent, (2) cancel 2-24 hours before (9 cases)—all cancelled, no reminder sent, (3) cancel after reminder was already sent (8 cases)—handled as edge case, (4) cancel on non-existent appointment (3 cases)—proper error responses, (5) double-cancel attempt (3 cases)—second attempt properly rejected. No crashes. One observation: under high concurrency (50 concurrent cancellations), Twilio API response times increased from 200ms to 450ms median, still well within timeout window (5s). No failed requests. Load test revealed no new bottlenecks. Repair verified complete. System ready for production.

---

ENTRY 9 | 2026-11-03
Limitations of evidence noted for record. All testing conducted on staging database with synthetic patron records; no real patron flow executed. Twilio cancellation API behavior verified in staging (sandbox credentials); production behavior not yet observed. SMS delivery timing not tested under library network conditions; only SendGrid SMTP tested, not actual library connectivity. Real-world patron behavior (e.g., cancellations during library hours vs. after-hours distribution) not modeled. Booking load at Riverside Branch historically low (est. 3-5 appointments per day); stress test used 50-120 concurrent operations, order of magnitude higher. UI confirmation modal not tested on actual library patron devices (only development machines and mobile emulators). These gaps are acceptable for a pilot; production readiness contingent on live-environment monitoring and incident response plan.

---

ENTRY 10 | 2026-11-05
Pilot launch window: 2026-11-10 to 2026-11-11 (internal trial, library staff only, 15 test appointments scheduled, not offered to public patrons). Pending Captain decision: proceed with internal trial as scheduled. If trial is postponed beyond 2026-11-11, the 15 booked test appointments must be cancelled manually, staff will lose scheduled testing windows, overlap with library's annual inventory event (2026-11-18) reduces available test time by 40%, and full public launch will slip from 2026-11-24 to 2026-12-08, compressing post-trial analysis window before holiday closure. Recommendation: proceed 2026-11-10. Awaiting approval.

# PROJECT LANTERN 2 STATUS REPORT
## Community Library Appointment Pilot

---

**2026-10-08 | ENTRY 1: PROJECT INITIATION**

Project Lantern 2 kicked off on schedule with full scope definition complete. The pilot aims to test an online appointment booking system for Meridian Valley Public Library's four branch locations. Scope covers: appointment scheduling for reference consultations (30-minute slots), study room reservations (60-minute slots), and computer lab access (45-minute slots). Target user population is 400 patrons across all branches. Backend infrastructure uses existing library database; frontend is web-based React application. Testing will run across three calendar weeks in November, culminating in a two-week internal trial with library staff. Team roster finalized: Marcus Webb (product), Yuki Tanaka (engineering lead), Priya Mendez (QA), David Cho (UX). Initial database schema validated against existing patron records. No blocking issues at launch.

---

**2026-10-15 | ENTRY 2: EARLY TESTING ENVIRONMENT READY**

Staging environment deployed successfully. All four branch locations now have test credentials configured in the database. Priya's QA team ran initial smoke tests: appointment creation, calendar rendering, time-slot conflict detection, and user authentication. Results: 47 test cases executed, 43 passed. Four failures identified were environment setup issues, not application bugs. Database performance baseline established: average query response time 140ms for availability checks, 95ms for slot booking. Redis caching layer tested with 500 concurrent user simulation; cache hit ratio 87% under normal load. Team identified need for additional testing on mobile browsers (iOS Safari, Android Chrome). Scheduled secondary round of compatibility testing for week of 2026-10-22. Preliminary documentation drafted for internal testers.

---

**2026-10-22 | ENTRY 3: USER ACCEPTANCE TESTING PHASE ONE COMPLETE**

First round of UAT concluded with 12 volunteer library staff members using the system for five days. Participants conducted 156 total booking transactions: 89 reference consultations, 51 study room reservations, 16 computer lab bookings. System stability solid; no crashes recorded. Users reported interface clarity as "good" or "excellent" in 94% of feedback surveys. Booking workflow intuitive for most; 11 of 12 participants completed first appointment without guidance. Mobile experience validated across iOS 17 and Android 14. Average booking time: 2 minutes 45 seconds from login to confirmation. One recurring user comment: unclear what happens after canceling an appointment. Three staff members reported confusion about whether cancellation email would auto-send. This prompted closer investigation into our cancellation flow logic.

---

**2026-10-28 | ENTRY 4: CANCELLATION FLOW GAP IDENTIFIED**

During post-UAT review, Yuki discovered a critical gap in the cancellation pathway. System allows users to cancel appointments with one-click confirmation, but the notification dispatch sequence has a hidden dependency: cancellation email triggers only after database record deletion completes, which happens asynchronously in a background job queue. In current testing, 87% of cancellations processed email within 60 seconds, but 13% show delays of 4-8 minutes. Worse: if patron closes browser immediately after clicking "confirm cancellation," they receive no visual confirmation that the action registered. No data loss occurs; the appointment is removed from the database correctly. However, user experience is ambiguous. Priya's logs revealed two UAT instances where patrons attempted to re-book the same slot, suggesting they doubted the cancellation succeeded. This gap was not caught in earlier testing because team did not explicitly test the cancellation scenario or measure email send latency under realistic timing conditions.

---

**2026-10-31 | ENTRY 5: ROOT CAUSE ANALYSIS AND REPAIR PLAN**

Root cause confirmed: the background job queue uses a standard FIFO processor with no prioritization tier. Cancellation notifications are treated identically to other transactional emails (appointment confirmations, reminder notifications). During peak testing hours (11:00-14:00), queue depth reached 320+ items, causing 10-minute total latencies. Secondary issue: user-facing confirmation message appears immediately after button click, but that message does not indicate whether email dispatch succeeded or is pending. Solution design approved: (1) separate cancellation emails into a priority queue; (2) add post-cancellation modal showing explicit confirmation status ("Email sent," "Sending...," or "Retry" if failure detected); (3) add retry logic for failed email sends within 5 minutes. Estimated implementation effort: 12 hours of engineering work plus 6 hours of QA validation. No database schema changes required. Yuki committed to delivery by 2026-11-05.

---

**2026-11-01 | ENTRY 6: CANCELLATION REPAIR IMPLEMENTATION BEGUN**

Yuki and junior engineer Raj Patel began implementing the three-part repair. Priority queue infrastructure deployed in staging; refactored email dispatcher to route cancellations to priority channel. Confirmation modal UI designed by David, approved by Marcus without design iteration. Modal includes three states: success (green checkmark, "Cancellation confirmed"), pending (spinner, "Sending confirmation..."), and retry prompt (orange warning, retry button). Implementation revealed one unexpected coupling: the existing appointment confirmation modal uses different visual language. Decided to update both modals to consistent design system rather than maintain two patterns. This added 2 hours to scope but reduces future maintenance debt. Retry logic completed; tested with simulated queue failures. Database indexes verified; no performance regression detected in staging. Code review scheduled for 2026-11-03. Current status: 68% complete.

---

**2026-11-03 | ENTRY 7: REPAIR VALIDATION AND EDGE CASE TESTING**

Repair code merged after peer review. Yuki and Priya executed expanded cancellation test suite: 247 cancellation transactions under varying conditions. Test matrix included: normal operation, queue under load (simulated 500-item backlog), email service degradation (50% delivery failure), network latency injection (250ms+ delays), and rapid re-booking attempts (user canceling and rebooking same slot within 30 seconds). Results: 243 of 247 tests passed. Four failures were retry-logic edge cases where a cancellation email failed, user clicked retry, but original record was already reprocessed. Fixed with idempotency key in email dispatch. Modal confirmation displayed correctly in 100% of test runs; state transitions smooth. Email latency under test load: 89% of cancellations now receive email within 12 seconds; 99th percentile latency is 35 seconds. Mobile modal rendering tested on iOS 17 and Android 14; no layout breakage. One unresolved issue: if user has notification delivery disabled in browser settings, no email is sent but modal still shows "Sending..." indefinitely (waiting for email system ACK). Noted as known limitation for post-launch iteration.

---

**2026-11-04 | ENTRY 8: EVIDENCE REVIEW AND TESTING LIMITATIONS**

QA team reviewed complete test evidence and identified scope limitations in our validation approach. Testing was conducted in staging with synthetic data (no real patron history, no production database load patterns). Simulated load testing used uniform random booking distribution; real library usage likely has temporal clustering (morning rush, lunch hour, evening). Email service testing used mock SMTP server; production uses Mailgun API with real network variability we cannot fully replicate. Only 4 of 12 original UAT participants available for repair validation; we did not retest with full original cohort. Mobile testing limited to two platforms; older Android versions (9-10) untested due to CI environment constraints. Retry logic was tested with injected failures but not against real email service degradation (e.g., Mailgun rate limits). These limitations are documented but do not invalidate the repair; they indicate that full confidence in cancellation reliability under real production conditions will only come after live monitoring post-launch. Proposed mitigation: add monitoring dashboard for email dispatch latency and failure rates, with alerting if 99th percentile exceeds 60 seconds.

---

**2026-11-05 | ENTRY 9: READINESS ASSESSMENT AND CAPTAIN DECISION PENDING**

Repair validation complete. System is ready for internal trial as scheduled. Cancellation flow now meets design criteria: user receives prompt visual confirmation, email delivery is prioritized and retried, and edge cases are documented. Marcus convened readiness review: no blocking issues remain. Proposed timeline: launch internal trial with library staff on 2026-11-12 for two weeks (through 2026-11-25). Trial will involve 25 staff testers rotating through all four branches, booking real appointments and canceling 20% of them to exercise repaired flow. Trial success criteria: (1) zero reported cancellation confirmation failures, (2) email delivery latency under 60 seconds for 99% of cancellations, (3) no crashes or data inconsistencies, (4) user satisfaction score 4.0+ out of 5. Marcus has flagged the trial schedule to the library director and is awaiting final approval. This decision rests with the library Captain (Director Eva Santos). Pending her confirmation by end of business 2026-11-05.

---

**2026-11-05 | ENTRY 10: TRIAL POSTPONEMENT IMPACT ANALYSIS**

If Director Santos postpones the internal trial beyond 2026-11-12, consequences cascade. Current team availability is constrained after 2026-11-25; Yuki transitions to a separate project (Building Initiative Q5 planning), and Priya has vacation scheduled 2026-11-26 through 2026-12-09. Restarting trial in December would require rebuilding test cohort and re-training new participants. Library branch closures 2026-12-20 through 2026-01-02 eliminate testing opportunity during peak winter patron activity. Postponement also delays go-live beyond target of 2026-12-15, pushing public availability into January when library seasonal usage dips, reducing real-world validation window. Public launch currently scheduled for 2026-12-22 assuming trial completes on time and no critical issues emerge. A two-week postponement compresses validation timeline and increases risk of launching with undetected production issues. Technical repairs are complete and stable; delay does not improve system quality. Team recommendation: proceed with trial on 2026-11-12 as planned. Awaiting Captain decision.

---

**END OF REPORT**

PROJECT LANTERN 3 - STATUS REPORT
Community Library Appointment Pilot
Reporting Period: 2026-10-01 through 2026-11-05

---

ENTRY 1 - 2026-10-01 - PROJECT KICKOFF AND SCOPE DEFINITION

Project Lantern 3 launched today with formal scope approval. The pilot targets three branch locations in the Riverside County library system: Central Downtown, Mill Creek Community, and Westridge Educational Hub. The system allows patrons to book reference librarian consultations, study room reservations, and technology training sessions through a web interface and SMS fallback. Scope includes appointment scheduling, patron notification via email and text, staff confirmation workflows, and basic reporting dashboards. The pilot runs for twelve weeks with target enrollment of 120 active patrons across all three branches. Success criteria are defined as ninety percent patron satisfaction on post-visit surveys, eighty-five percent on-time arrival rates, and zero critical system failures during operating hours. Staff capacity is three full-time developers, one QA engineer, two library liaison managers, and rotating librarian stakeholder participation. Budget allocation covers development infrastructure, SMS gateway costs, and staff time through December 2026. Expected completion is feature-complete by 2026-11-15 with live traffic acceptance running through 2026-12-20.

---

ENTRY 2 - 2026-10-08 - INITIAL SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE AND COMPONENT TESTING

Development completed the core system architecture this week. The appointment booking engine accepts reservations through three channels: web portal, phone hotline with voice menu, and email request with automated parsing. The backend uses PostgreSQL for appointment storage with redundant backups. Frontend styling follows county accessibility standards, WCAG 2.1 AA compliance validated at component level. Automated test suite for booking logic reached eighty-two percent code coverage with unit tests for time conflict detection, timezone handling, and patron eligibility validation. Manual testing began on the web interface with three test scenarios per librarian role: reference consultant, facilities coordinator, and branch supervisor. Initial accessibility audit showed five minor color contrast issues and two missing alt text labels, all tagged for remediation. SMS notification service integrated with Twilio using production credentials in sandbox mode. First mock appointment cycle completed successfully with fifty test bookings, automated confirmations, and reminders working as designed. Staff conducted initial usability interviews with eight library employees, collecting feedback on dashboard navigation and reporting features.

---

ENTRY 3 - 2026-10-15 - EXTENDED INTEGRATION TESTING AND PATRON WORKFLOW DISCOVERY

Extended integration testing revealed the interconnection between appointment confirmation and the patron information database. A complete end-to-end workflow was tested: patron books appointment via web portal, system validates availability, patron receives email confirmation with calendar invite, librarian receives staff notification, appointment appears on branch calendar, and reminder SMS sends twenty-four hours before scheduled time. Testing uncovered a minor race condition when two patrons booked the same time slot simultaneously, now fixed by adding database-level locking. The team conducted two rounds of user acceptance testing with twelve volunteer patrons from the local community, each completing four test bookings across different appointment types. Patrons reported average task completion time of four minutes for web booking and seven minutes for phone booking due to menu navigation. The reporting dashboard was tested with six months of simulated historical data, showing capacity utilization charts, no-show analysis, and patron retention trends. One integration point required rework: the study room availability feed was initially pulling stale data from a nightly batch job, now replaced with real-time queries. Staff conducted competency training with all three branch locations, covering appointment approval workflows, patron communication, and emergency cancellation procedures.

---

ENTRY 4 - 2026-10-22 - DISCOVERY OF CANCELLATION FLOW GAP AND IMPACT ASSESSMENT

A critical workflow gap was discovered during stress testing this week. The cancellation flow had no defined handling for cases where a patron cancels within two hours of their appointment time. Current system sends a notification to the librarian but does not automatically open the time slot for rebooking; the slot remains marked as reserved but empty. Manual reclassification requires librarian intervention in the admin panel, which takes approximately eight minutes per incident. Testing simulated one hundred cancellations with varying time windows. Results showed that forty-two percent of cancellations occurred within four hours of appointment time, with fifteen percent occurring less than two hours before. If librarians miss reclassifying a slot, the appointment calendar shows false occupancy for that day, blocking new patron bookings. This directly conflicts with the scope requirement for appointment availability accuracy. Additionally, duplicate cancellation requests can occur when patrons use both the web portal and phone hotline, causing data inconsistency. The QA team documented three scenarios where this occurred during testing, each requiring manual database correction. The gap creates downstream reporting errors: no-show counts include unavailable librarians, utilization rates appear artificially low, and capacity planning dashboards show inaccurate demand patterns.

---

ENTRY 5 - 2026-10-29 - CANCELLATION FLOW REPAIR IMPLEMENTATION AND VERIFICATION

The cancellation flow repair was implemented and tested this week. The solution includes three components: an automated time-slot re-opening mechanism that triggers immediately upon patron cancellation regardless of timing, a duplicate-request guard using idempotent operation keys in the database, and a librarian notification system that batches slot openings into a single daily summary email rather than individual interruptions. The automated mechanism was built using a SQL trigger that executes transactionally when a cancellation record is inserted, ensuring atomic updates. The duplicate guard checks for existing cancellation requests from the same patron for the same appointment within a one-minute window, preventing accidental re-submissions. Testing of the repair included regression suite execution with fifteen hundred appointment lifecycle scenarios, covering all combinations of booking, confirmation, reminder, and cancellation. The automated reclassification was validated against manual reclassification in five hundred test cases, confirming identical results. Performance testing showed the new trigger adds less than one millisecond to the cancellation operation. The team tested edge cases including same-day rebooking by the original patron, cascading cancellations when a librarian cancels, and concurrent cancellation requests from the system and patron. All cases now process without manual intervention. QA conducted two verification cycles with the librarian staff using live data from the volunteer patron testing, confirming that no manual reclassification occurred in seventy-eight test cancellations across the four-hour and two-hour windows.

---

ENTRY 6 - 2026-11-01 - EVIDENCE LIMITATIONS AND DATA QUALITY CONSTRAINTS

Documentation of evidence limitations and data quality constraints was completed this week to ensure realistic scope of validation claims. The volunteer patron pool includes only forty-two individuals who responded to community outreach, predominantly in the age range thirty-five to sixty-five; younger patrons and non-English speakers are underrepresented. Simulated historical data used in testing was generated synthetically based on assumptions about typical library traffic patterns and seasonal variation; no actual patron behavior data from equivalent systems was available for calibration. Testing conducted in controlled environments with dedicated test accounts does not replicate real network conditions, concurrent user loads beyond fifty simultaneous users, or mobile network quality variance. SMS delivery reliability was tested only with Twilio sandbox endpoints; production SMS behavior depends on carrier routing decisions outside system scope. The automated cancellation trigger was tested with PostgreSQL version thirteen; library systems use version twelve in production, and backward compatibility cannot be fully verified without production deployment. Staff competency training covered only three specific branches; two additional branches may join the pilot after week six if enrollment targets are met, and their staff training needs may differ. The accessibility audit was conducted remotely using automated scanning and manual spot-checks; in-person testing with users who have visual or motor disabilities has not occurred. Calendar invite integration depends on email client software at patron's home; delivery success rates depend on spam filter tuning, proxy server configuration, and other elements outside project scope.

---

ENTRY 7 - 2026-11-02 - PREPARATION FOR INTERNAL TRIAL AND SCOPE CONFIRMATION

The project is ready for internal trial commencement with formal scope confirmation completed. Internal trial will run for two weeks using real patron traffic at Central Downtown branch location only, with volunteer staff participation. The trial will operate during extended hours Monday through Saturday, ten a.m. through six p.m., with librarian coverage by four scheduled staff members. Trial success criteria include: zero critical system failures, response time under three seconds for ninety-fifth percentile requests, automated cancellation reclassification occurring in one hundred percent of late cancellations without manual intervention, patron satisfaction survey average of four point two or higher on five-point scale, and staff satisfaction survey confirming workflow integration feasibility. Data collection during trial includes response time telemetry, error logs, patron satisfaction surveys administered on-site with QR code linking to online form, staff feedback sessions scheduled for days four, nine, and fourteen, and hourly system utilization reporting. The trial is resource-intensive: full QA presence on-site for first three days, on-call support for remaining eleven days, daily report generation and analysis, and staff coordination meetings every other day. Trial commencement requires Captain approval and final sign-off on resource allocation. If trial is postponed by one week, the project completion deadline compresses to four weeks, eliminating the planned two-week contingency period and eliminating the secondary branch testing phase originally scheduled for weeks nine through eleven.

---

ENTRY 8 - 2026-11-03 - PENDING CAPTAIN DECISION BRIEFING

Captain decision required this week on internal trial commencement timing and scope. Two decisions are coupled: approval to start the internal trial on 2026-11-06 depends on confirming resource availability from existing development staff, and this allocation directly impacts secondary branch on-site training completion by 2026-11-12. The trial will consume thirty percent of QA capacity, twenty percent of developer time for on-call support, and one hundred percent of one liaison manager for coordination. Development schedule shows three feature items remain as stretch goals: advanced reporting with custom date ranges, bulk appointment import for partner organizations, and patron preference persistence across sessions. These will be deferred if trial proceeds as scheduled; if trial is postponed, these items can complete in parallel during trial preparation extension. The decision framework: confirm trial start date by 2026-11-05 end of business, or communicate delay to volunteer partners with revised timeline. If trial is postponed by one week, the project absorbs the delay into week nine, compressing the post-trial adjustment period from ten days to three days and eliminating planned staff retraining on system improvements identified during trial.

---

ENTRY 9 - 2026-11-04 - TRIAL READINESS VERIFICATION AND DOCUMENTATION

Trial readiness verification completed today with all checklist items passing. Production environment configured with dedicated database instance, SSL certificates valid through 2027, backup schedule set for daily execution, and disaster recovery procedures documented with recovery time objective of two hours. Monitoring dashboard set up tracking system response times, error rates, database connection counts, SMS delivery status, and email transmission logs. On-call support contacts established with escalation path: QA engineer first, tech lead second, project manager third. Client communication template prepared for daily trial reports sent to library administration, covering usage statistics, any issues encountered, and emerging requirements. Volunteer staff completed three-hour orientation covering system navigation, staff workflows, patron communication, and emergency procedures. Orientation completion rate: one hundred percent of scheduled staff, with proficiency test average score of eighty-six percent. All staff demonstrated competency with appointment approval workflow. Documentation finalized: technical architecture guide, staff user manual with screenshots, troubleshooting guide for common issues, patron quick-start guide, and administrative procedures for settings changes. Communication sent to enrolled patrons explaining trial expectations, system features, and feedback survey process. Volunteer patron response rate to survey pre-trial questions: sixty-seven percent completion rate. Technical validation complete: system load testing showed capacity for one hundred fifty concurrent users without performance degradation, database query optimization reduced average response time to one point eight seconds, and error recovery procedures tested across five failure scenarios with all tests passing.

---

As the pilot progressed through weeks two and three, the team identified evidence limitations affecting confidence in the system's reliability claims. Bryn Hardwick documented these in a detailed report:

First limitation: SendGrid webhook events (bounce, permanent failure, complaint) arrive asynchronously and are not guaranteed to arrive. The SendGrid documentation states that webhooks are delivered with a minimum of 100 retries over 24 hours if delivery fails, but there is a small possibility (estimated <0.1% by SendGrid) that a bounce event never arrives. This means a cancellation email that actually failed to deliver might never be marked as failed in the email_log table, and no fallback notification would be triggered. The team's retry-and-fallback system assumes webhooks arrive. If webhooks fail silently, the gap persists.

Second limitation: the staff end-of-day summary email that lists failed cancellation notifications is sent via SendGrid, using the same service that may have failed to deliver the original cancellation email. If the branch manager's email address is on a blocklist or has a failing mailbox, the summary email itself will fail to deliver. The team would not know the branch manager did not receive it. This is a second-order failure mode.

Third limitation: the pilot data volume (127 bookings, 11 cancellations over week one-two) is insufficient to validate reliability at production scale. At full scale, the library system might handle 800+ appointments per month across all branches. The test coverage assumes failure rates of 1-3 per 200 events, but actual failure rates at scale may differ. Production email services experience lower failure rates under normal circumstances but can experience rapid increases during outages.

Fourth limitation: the time zone detection feature (Nia Patel's browser-based Intl API implementation) was tested only in Bryn Hardwick's local time zone (America/New_York). The system has not been tested during daylight saving time transitions. In March 2027 and November 2027, patron time zones will shift. It is unknown whether the browser-based time detection will remain accurate after the transition, or whether patrons will see incorrect time slots.

Fifth limitation: the cancellation email template includes patron name, appointment date, time, branch, and service. The template was designed for English-speaking patrons. The pilot serves Riverside (diverse immigrant population), Cathedral Hill (university neighborhood), and Lakeshore (residential). No translation was done. Non-English-speaking patrons may not understand the cancellation notification. This is a scope limitation (translation is out-of-scope for the pilot) but represents a real usability gap.

Sixth limitation: staff user roles and permissions are stored in the staff_roles table with a permissions column (free text or enum). The design does not enforce role-based access control (RBAC) at the code level. A branch staff member should see only appointments for their branch, but this is implemented via filtering in the JavaScript frontend, not in the backend API. A malicious actor could inspect network traffic, modify branch IDs, and potentially view or modify appointments for other branches. The team decided to defer RBAC security hardening to post-pilot.

Test suite results: 58 of 62 tests passed; 4 remain under investigation due to timeout delays in concurrent cancellation attempts under simulated load. Load testing with 200 concurrent users placing and cancelling holds simultaneously revealed latency spikes in the 2.5 to 3.2 second range when more than 80 patrons triggered cancellations within a 10-second window. Nominal single-user cancellation latency is 180 milliseconds, well within acceptable bounds. The timeout failures occur only when the database connection pool reaches 95% capacity; these are not data corruption events but rather throttling under extreme concurrent load unlikely in normal Riverside branch operations (maximum historical concurrent patrons: 34). Miriam Chen re-ran all five of her original discovery scenarios: all cancellations now execute correctly, hold status updates propagate to the patron interface within 500 milliseconds, and staff see the released materials immediately in the reassignment queue. Two staff members (Gary Voss and Pam Ng) conducted end-to-end workflow testing in the staging environment Friday, completing 30 practice cycles of placement, fulfillment, and cancellation across different material types. Both reported the interface was intuitive and the workflow faster than the legacy manual process. Database audit trail was verified: all 92 test cancellations appear with correct timestamps and patron identifiers. Backup and restore procedures tested successfully Saturday evening; a full holds table snapshot and recovery completed in 4 minutes 15 seconds, within our 5-minute acceptable window. No data loss observed in any scenario.

2026-11-03 - Known Limitation: Concurrent Booking on Single Material

During load testing Friday, a fictional limitation emerged in the system behavior when multiple patrons attempt to book the same item simultaneously. The booking engine currently supports only sequential holds on individual copies; when a material has three physical copies and four patrons submit booking requests within the same second, the fourth patron receives a "no availability" response even though one copy technically remains unclaimed. The system lacks a dynamic re-queuing algorithm to assign the fourth patron to the next available copy or place them in a hold queue that auto-assigns when another copy arrives back in the system. This is a known design limitation accepted in the original requirements but not prioritized for the pilot phase. Impact: patrons may experience a perceived unavailability that contradicts the catalog display, requiring them to retry their booking within a few seconds for the system to recognize updated inventory. Staff have been trained to explain this behavior and assist patrons with manual rebooking if needed. The engineering team flagged this as a future optimization candidate (estimated effort: 8 to 12 engineering hours for a full queue-aware assignment algorithm). For the trial scope, we accept this limitation because Riverside branch average daily patron traffic is lower than the peak concurrent scenario that triggers the issue, and the workaround is simple. Monitoring will track how often patrons encounter this state and whether user satisfaction metrics are affected. If more than 3% of booking attempts result in spurious unavailability, the limitation will be reassessed before the phase-two expansion to other branches.

All conditions are now in place. The pilot will run for eight weeks, ending December 30, 2026, with interim review gates at weeks two and four. The treatment group (170 patrons) will use the new booking interface. Staff at Riverside have completed training and signed off on operational readiness. 2026-10-22 — Missing Cancellation Path Discovered in Testing

During internal acceptance testing, tester Priya Desai flagged a critical gap: the booking system lacked any cancellation mechanism. Users could view their confirmed reservations in the dashboard but had no way to cancel them through the interface. The only workaround was a manual email to staff at each branch, which defeats the automation goal entirely. Cancellation requests represented 18% of all estimated transactions in the pilot design phase, so this was a significant oversight. The issue originated in the requirements document, where cancellation was marked as a phase-two feature but never escalated when phase one went into final development. The implications were severe: if a patron booked incorrectly or circumstances changed, they would need staff intervention, creating support overhead and poor user experience. We assessed delaying the trial, but the pilot schedule was already committed to other branch initiatives. Instead, we committed to a one-week fix-and-verify cycle, pushing the trial start from 2026-10-29 to 2026-11-05. Cancellation design required careful thought because cancellations create orphaned reservation slots that need immediate reuse availability, and we needed to prevent double-cancellation attempts. The team documented three design options: a simple hard-delete with reuse flagging, a soft-delete with a 24-hour undo window, and a cancellation-request workflow requiring staff approval. We selected the hard-delete approach with 30-second reuse delay to minimize complexity during pilot.

2026-10-25 — Cancellation Build and Unit Test Completion

Marcus Webb completed the cancellation endpoint build by end of day 2026-10-24. The implementation added a DELETE /bookings/{booking_id} endpoint that checks the booking exists, validates the user owns it, cancels it, and returns freed availability to the pool with a 30-second hold-release timer. Unit tests covered happy path cancellation, non-existent booking rejection, permission denial when a different user attempts cancellation, and slot reuse timing. Test coverage reached 94% for the new cancellation module. All unit tests passed on first run. Kenji Sato then conducted manual integration testing on the staging environment with realistic data: he created five test bookings across different branches and times, cancelled three of them, and verified that the slots reappeared in availability displays within the expected window. Email notifications were triggered correctly for cancellations, with subject line "Reservation Cancelled" and confirmation of freed time. One edge case emerged: if a user cancelled a booking and immediately rebooked the same slot, the database timestamp conflicts created a millisecond race condition where both transactions could claim the slot. Marcus added a pessimistic lock during the 30-second release window to prevent this. Test re-run with 50 rapid cancel-and-rebook sequences showed zero conflicts. One minor issue surfaced: the staff-facing utilization dashboard did not immediately reflect cancelled slots in aggregated metrics, showing a 2-minute lag before the counts updated. This was acceptable for pilot use but noted as a performance optimization for a future release. Database query logs showed the cancellation queries were well-indexed and not creating table locks. We also tested cancellation behavior during off-hours: the system properly rejected cancellations after 22:00 on Fridays for weekend bookings that the Riverside branch policy prevents modifying. This constraint was correctly enforced. Kenji verified the patron surveys contained no questions about cancellation since it was previously unavailable, so we added three questions to the week-one survey asking specifically about cancellation usability and timing. The current system allows staff to view all bookings made by patrons but has no administrative cancellation capability. If a room becomes unavailable due to maintenance or a scheduling conflict emerges at the branch level, staff must contact each affected patron individually or request a technical override from Marcus. In the pilot scope, this affects fewer than five anticipated scenarios, so we marked it as an acceptable pilot limitation with a ticket for phase-two work. The design decision was intentional: granting staff delete permissions on patron bookings raised data-governance questions that needed legal review, which was not scheduled before pilot launch. We documented the workaround: staff can note the unavailable room in the system comments section, and patrons will see a warning flag. For the pilot window, this is sufficient because branch maintenance is scheduled around pilot dates. Kenji confirmed that no maintenance is planned at Meadowside or Riverside until 2026-12-01, well after pilot conclusion on 2026-11-29. The limitation was disclosed to pilot staff during their training session on 2026-10-30. No staff member raised concerns during the Q&A. Captain Marcus Torrance reviewed the final pilot readiness report today and approved launch for tomorrow, 2026-11-05, with the green path: no postponement. Testing infrastructure remains live as a fallback, and Marcus maintains a ready rollback procedure for critical issues, though no rollback to date has been necessary during staging activities. All commitments are met. Trial commences on schedule.

PROJECT PEBBLE 16 STATUS REPORT
Internal Library-Booking Trial

2026-10-08

Project Pebble 16 pilot scope approved by Captain Morgan. Trial planned to test in-house library equipment booking system across four pilot teams: Editorial, Data, Systems, and Facilities. Scope includes reservation creation, real-time availability view, and cancellation workflow. Booking window opens 7 days forward, closes 2 hours before session start. Pilot runs 30 days in controlled environment before org-wide rollout. Team lead assigned: Chen Wei. Infrastructure uses existing PostgreSQL cluster in AWS us-west-2, frontend React-based, backend Node.js microservice. Bootstrap data loaded 2026-10-07 with 187 equipment items mapped across 12 physical locations. Trial success metric: 95% of team member bookings completed without manual intervention. Known constraint: email notification service still in staging, only Slack alerts currently live. Kickoff meeting held with all four pilot team leads. Next step: validation of equipment catalog accuracy and booking time-slot calculation logic.

2026-10-14

Critical issue discovered during dry-run test. User workflow gap identified: users can create bookings and view reservations, but no cancellation path exists in the UI. User attempting to cancel a 2026-10-15 equipment booking found no button, no menu option, no documented process. Backend API endpoint exists (/api/bookings/:id/cancel) but frontend never calls it. This blocks trial start—team members will not accept a system with no undo path. Duration of issue unknown; code review shows cancellation endpoint was built 2026-09-28 but feature branch never merged to main. Responsible engineer unreachable for 48 hours. Captain Morgan flagged for awareness. Scope impact: moderate. Trial start postponed pending fix. Temporary workaround documented for pilot users: email chen-wei@company with booking ID and reason; manual cancellation performed server-side. Not acceptable as permanent solution. Recovery plan: implement cancellation button in booking list view, connect to existing API, run full regression suite, obtain Captain approval before trial restart.

2026-10-18

Cancellation button implementation complete. Code committed 2026-10-17 22:34 UTC by Chen Wei. Changes: new Cancel button added to each reservation card in booking list component, calls /api/bookings/:id/cancel with authorization header, displays confirmation modal before sending request, updates local state and refetches booking list on success. Button disabled if booking time falls within 2-hour pre-session window (hardcoded policy). Manual testing completed across Chrome 128, Firefox 123, Safari 17. Cancel action tested on 23 different bookings: success rate 100%. Cancellation confirmation email template deployed but notification still routing to Slack pending; email will backfill when staging service moves to production 2026-10-25. Edge case: user cancels booking, immediately re-books same slot. Behavior verified correct—cancellation committed immediately, slot released for rebooking within same transaction. One minor UX issue found: button text "Cancel Booking" truncates on mobile screens <360px width. Fixed 2026-10-18 11:15 UTC, button now wraps to two lines. Trial restart target: 2026-10-21.

2026-10-21

Regression test suite executed across 47 test cases covering booking creation, updates, cancellations, and concurrent user scenarios. Results: 46 pass, 1 fail. Failing test: concurrent_cancel_rebook_sequence. Scenario: User A cancels booking at 10:15:03.447 UTC, User B rebooking request arrives 10:15:03.451 UTC (4 milliseconds later). Race condition: both requests read slot availability state before either write commits. User B receives slot confirmation, but slot already allocated to User A's immediate rebook. Duplication detected in downstream booking list query, caught by test assertion. Root cause: database transaction isolation level set to READ_COMMITTED instead of SERIALIZABLE. Fix applied: updated booking service cancellation handler to use SERIALIZABLE isolation. Retest performed 15 times across time-shifted booking windows; race condition no longer reproduced. Secondary check: load test with 120 concurrent users booking across 50 time slots over 5-minute window. No failures observed. Trial restart approved by Captain Morgan 2026-10-21 18:42 UTC. Trial officially begins 2026-10-22 06:00 UTC across four pilot teams.

2026-10-29

Trial day seven complete. 287 total bookings created, 43 cancellations processed, zero booking conflicts reported. System response time averaged 240ms for booking creation, 180ms for list retrieval, 195ms for cancellations. No downtime incidents. User feedback collected via Slack surveys: 89% satisfaction rating, primary praise centered on real-time availability and clean UI. One recurring limitation surfaced: system does not support booking recurrence or series. Users reported manual workaround of creating individual bookings for weekly recurring needs—12 team members each creating 4 bookings per month for standing meetings with equipment. This represents false load on the system and creates cancellation risk if one week's booking forgotten. Requests filed for repeating booking feature in backlog, but scope explicitly excluded from pilot. Documented as known limit and will inform phase-two planning. No blocker to trial continuation. Second regression suite run completed 2026-10-28: 47 pass, 0 fail. Database transaction logs reviewed; no anomalies detected. All four pilot teams remain active and engaged. Trial continuation approved through 2026-11-21.

2026-11-05

Trial day twenty-three. Cumulative metrics: 612 bookings, 103 cancellations, zero system errors in error logs. Response time metrics stable. One booking system outage 2026-11-02 04:17 UTC caused by AWS RDS maintenance window—5 minute downtime, system returned online automatically. Recommendation: proceed with trial-to-production transition with recurrence feature prioritized for phase-two roadmap. Captain decision received 2026-11-05 08:22 UTC: trial greenlit for production launch 2026-11-17 across all company departments. Scope: all 34 business units, all 7 office locations, full equipment catalog including external vendor rentals. Expected user base: 1,840 active team members. Infrastructure scaling completed 2026-11-04. Team assignments finalized. Production launch preparation begins immediately.
